candidates.topic: Mantis shrimp can see 16 types of color
candidates.teaser: You think you see colors well? This tiny sea creature makes your eyes look completely broken.
candidates.video_title: This Shrimp Sees Colors You Can't Even Imagine
candidates.video_description: The mantis shrimp has 16 types of color receptors, compared to just 3 in humans. Its vision is so advanced that scientists are studying it to build better cameras and medical scanners.
candidates.script: What if I told you there's a creature that can see colors your brain can't even process? Humans have 3 types of color receptors in our eyes. The mantis shrimp has 16. Sixteen. It can detect ultraviolet light, infrared, and colors that literally have no name in any human language. Scientists are so amazed by its eyes that they're using them as a blueprint for cancer-detecting cameras. This tiny shrimp, no bigger than your hand, sees a version of reality we will never experience. So here's the question — if a shrimp sees 16 colors and we only see 3, what else are we completely blind to?

candidates.topic: Cleopatra's needle obelisk hidden time capsule
candidates.teaser: There's a secret box buried under one of the most famous monuments in New York — and most people walk right past it every day.
candidates.video_title: A Secret Time Capsule Is Hidden in Central Park
candidates.video_description: Beneath the ancient Egyptian obelisk in Central Park lies a buried time capsule from 1880, filled with newspapers, coins, and a census. Almost no one knows it exists.
candidates.script: There is a secret box buried right beneath Central Park, and almost nobody knows it exists. In 1880, when workers installed the ancient Egyptian obelisk known as Cleopatra's Needle in New York City, they buried a time capsule directly underneath it. Inside? A copy of the Declaration of Independence, a Bible, a US census, coins, newspapers, and even a guide to the English language. It has been sitting under millions of tourists' feet for over 140 years, completely untouched. No one has opened it since. So the real question is — what would you put inside a time capsule meant to last another 140 years?

candidates.topic: Trees can recognize their own kin
candidates.teaser: Trees don't just grow — they actually recognize their own children and treat them differently than strangers.
candidates.video_title: Trees Know Who Their Children Are. Seriously.
candidates.video_description: Research shows that trees can identify their own seedlings through root chemicals and deliberately share nutrients with them. They essentially play favorites — and science can prove it.
candidates.script: Trees can recognize their own children — and this isn't a metaphor. Scientists discovered that mother trees identify their own seedlings through chemical signals in the roots. Once recognized, the mother tree actually redirects extra nutrients specifically to her offspring, giving them a survival advantage over unrelated seedlings growing right beside them. Researcher Suzanne Simard called these hub trees 'mother trees,' and found that when they are cut down, the surrounding young trees survival rate drops dramatically. A forest is not just a collection of plants. It is a family. So next time you walk through the woods, ask yourself — are you the stranger, or are you being watched?

candidates.topic: The first computer bug was a real insect
candidates.teaser: The reason we call software problems 'bugs' today started with an actual dead insect found inside a computer in 1947.
candidates.video_title: The First Computer 'Bug' Was a Real Insect
candidates.video_description: In 1947, engineers found a moth stuck inside a Harvard computer causing errors. They taped it into their logbook and wrote 'first actual case of bug being found.' The word stuck forever.
candidates.script: Every time your phone crashes or an app freezes, you blame a 'bug.' But do you know why we actually call it that? In 1947, engineers working on the Harvard Mark II computer found it was producing errors. When they opened the machine to investigate, they found a real moth — a dead moth — trapped between the relay contacts, causing the malfunction. They taped it into their logbook and wrote: 'first actual case of bug being found.' That logbook still exists today at the Smithsonian Institution. One dead moth gave a name to every software problem in human history. What other tech terms do you think have a weird origin story like this?

candidates.topic: You are taller in the morning than at night
candidates.teaser: Your height changes every single day — and by more than you'd ever guess.
candidates.video_title: You're Actually Taller in the Morning Than at Night
candidates.video_description: The cartilage between your spinal discs compresses throughout the day under gravity, making you up to 1.5 cm shorter by evening. You grow back while you sleep.
candidates.script: When you wake up tomorrow morning, you will be taller than you are right now — by up to one and a half centimeters. Throughout the day, gravity constantly compresses the cartilage between your spinal discs. Every step you take, every hour you sit or stand, that soft tissue gets squeezed thinner and thinner. By evening, you've lost measurable height. But while you sleep horizontally, the pressure disappears, and the cartilage slowly expands back to its original size. Astronauts in zero gravity actually grow up to 5 centimeters taller in space because gravity never pulls them down at all. So technically, your true height? Nobody has ever accurately measured it.
